title: Semisimple rank from a maximal torus and the radical
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Use reductivity, maximal tori, and scheme-theoretic centralizer points as in [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]. A torus is a group isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for an integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $H$ be reductive and let $T\subseteq H$ be a maximal torus. Let $R\subseteq H$ be a central torus which contains every smooth connected solvable normal subgroup of $H$, and let $Q=H/R$ be the represented fppf quotient of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. Here solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial, and the fppf quotient means sheafification of $A\mapsto H(A)/R(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. Every central torus of $H$ is contained in $T$; in particular $R\subseteq T$. The quotient torus $T/R$ is a maximal torus of $Q$, and $$\operatorname{rank}(Q)=\dim T-\dim R.$$ Rank means the dimension of a maximal torus, dimension means Krull dimension of the scheme, and this rank of $Q$ is the semisimple rank of $H$.

source.place: Proposition 17.20 (images of maximal tori under quotient maps), printed pp.357--358; Corollaries 17.61--17.62, printed pp.372--373; Definition 19.20 and Proposition 19.21(a), printed pp.401--402. The radical is the central torus, so dim R = dim Z(H).

proof.text: Let $C\subseteq H$ be any central torus. For every commutative $F$-algebra $A$, each $c\in C(A)$ commutes with every $t\in T(B)$ after every $A$-algebra extension $B$. Thus $C(A)\subseteq C_H(T)(A)$. The scheme-theoretic equality $C_H(T)=T$ from [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer] applies because $F$ is algebraically closed, $H$ is reductive, and $T$ is maximal. Consequently the inclusion of subgroup functors $C\subseteq H$ factors through $T\subseteq H$. This proves $C\subseteq T$ as subgroup schemes, and in particular $R\subseteq T$.

The tori $T$ and $R$ are smooth and connected by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus]. Since $R$ is central it is normal in $H$. Apply [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] to $R\subseteq H$. It gives a quotient homomorphism $q:H\to Q$ which is faithfully flat and finitely presented, with scheme-theoretic kernel $R$. It also gives that $Q$ is affine, finite type, smooth and connected, since reductivity includes smoothness and connectedness of $H$. Thus $q$ satisfies the smooth connected group hypotheses needed for the maximal-torus image theorem.

source.place: Definition 12.14 and following paragraph, p.236; Propositions 5.25--5.29, p.105

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-quotient-borel-torus-images] to $q$ and $T$. Its scheme-theoretic image $S=q(T)$ is a maximal torus of $Q$, and $q_T:T\to S$ is faithfully flat. The kernel of $q|_T:T\to Q$ is the scheme-theoretic intersection $T\cap\ker q=T\cap R=R$, using Step 1. The homomorphism theorem [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] identifies the image of this homomorphism with its represented fppf quotient by the kernel, hence gives $T/R\simeq S$, compatibly with the homomorphisms into $Q$. In particular $T/R$, viewed through this closed inclusion in $Q$, is the maximal torus $S$.

source.place: Proposition 17.20, pp.357--358; Theorem 5.39 and Remark 5.42, p.108

proof.text: Let the smooth connected affine group $T$ act on the affine finite-type scheme $S$ by $t\cdot s=q_T(t)s$. The homomorphism identity for $q_T$ and the group identities give the action identities. The orbit map of $1\in S(F)$ is $q_T$, which is surjective; thus its orbit $O_1$ has underlying topological space $|S|$. For every commutative $F$-algebra $A$, its stabilizer consists exactly of the $t\in T(A)$ with $q_T(t)=1$, so the scheme-theoretic stabilizer is $R$, including on nonreduced algebras. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry] with acting group $T$, target $S$ and point $1$: it gives $\dim O_1=\dim T-\dim R$. Krull dimension depends only on the underlying topological space, by [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], so $\dim S=\dim O_1$. This argument requires no identification of an orbit with a possibly nonreduced image as schemes.

source.place: Propositions 7.4 and 7.11, pp.139--141, and Proposition 5.23, p.104

proof.text: Since $S\simeq T/R$ is a maximal torus of $Q$, the stated definition of rank gives $\operatorname{rank}(Q)=\dim S=\dim T-\dim R$. Finally $R$ is smooth and connected by Step 2, is normal by centrality, and is solvable because it is commutative: on every test algebra it is a product of groups of units, whose commutators are $1$. Together with the hypothesis that $R$ contains every smooth connected solvable normal subgroup of $H$, this says exactly that $R$ is the radical of $H$. Therefore the rank of $Q=H/R$ is the semisimple rank of $H$, as in Definition 19.20.

proof_origin.place: Propositions 17.61 and 17.20; Definition 19.20 and Proposition 19.21(a), with quotient identification (Theorem 5.39) and quotient dimension (Propositions 5.23 and 7.11) made explicit.
